implementation_notes: Swift's Sequence protocol plus the lazy view give the in-process pipeline: calling .lazy on a collection returns a LazySequence whose stages (filter, map, compactMap, prefix) are evaluated per element at iteration time, so no intermediate arrays are built; the stage interface is a closure over Element and the sequence is the pipe. Array's filter/map are eager and allocate one array per stage, which is the trap. Prefer Combine or AsyncSequence when values arrive asynchronously from a network, timer or UI source.
code_sketch:
let pipeline = records.lazy                   // lazy view, no array built
    .filter { !$0.isDraft }                   // stage 1
    .map { $0.applyingTax(rate) }             // stage 2

for invoice in pipeline {                      // per-element evaluation
    sink.write(invoice)
}
pitfalls: Dropping .lazy silently reintroduces one array per stage, while calling .lazy without a strict consumer (for-in, Array(...), reduce) means the work never happens.
Lazy views keep a reference to their base collection, so iterating a view of a temporary keeps it alive and can observe later mutations of a reference type.

variants.name: Combine publisher operator chain
variants.implementation_notes: Combine turns a stage into an operator on a Publisher: map, filter, compactMap, flatMap and friends compose declaratively, consuming the chain requires a subscription (sink/assign), and backpressure is expressed as Subscribers.Demand, so the pipeline requests only what downstream can take. This is the realization for event-shaped asynchronous data (network responses, timers, notifications, UI state) where stages must be cancellable and hot; lazy Sequences remain the right tool for pure in-memory transformations because publishers add subscription and demand machinery.
variants.code_sketch:
let pipeline = URLSession.shared.dataTaskPublisher(for: url)
    .map(\.data)                                     // stage 1
    .filter { !$0.isEmpty }                          // stage 2
    .decode(type: [Record].self, decoder: JSONDecoder())
    .map { $0.filter(\.valid) }                      // stage 3

let token = pipeline.sink(receiveCompletion: { print($0) },
                          receiveValue: { sink.write($0) })
pitfalls: A subscription without a retained AnyCancellable is cancelled immediately, so the pipeline appears to produce nothing.
An error terminates a publisher chain permanently; a failing stage must be isolated with catch/flatMap/retry so the rest of the flow can continue.
Demand is easy to get wrong in custom publishers: requesting unbounded demand from a slow source discards the backpressure the pattern relies on.

variants.name: AsyncSequence stages with for await
variants.idiom_name: AsyncStream source plus map/filter operators consumed with for await
variants.implementation_notes: Swift 5.5's AsyncSequence mirrors the sequence pipeline for asynchronous producers: a stage is an async sequence (built with AsyncStream, or composed with the standard library's map/filter/prefix operators) and for await consumes it, suspending the consumer so the producer is naturally paced - the pull side of the pattern applied to asynchronous data. Combine it with structured concurrency (Task trees, task groups) so cancellation propagates through the chain; use the synchronous lazy sequence when there is nothing to await.
pitfalls: An AsyncStream continuation with an unbounded buffering policy ignores backpressure and accumulates elements in memory; choose a bounded policy and decide the overflow behaviour.
Async sequences are single-pass: iterating the same sequence twice does not replay values, and concurrent iteration of one sequence is not supported.
Cancelling the surrounding Task cancels the for await loop but not producers that ignore cancellation - their continuations must be finished explicitly.
